## 4. Serving and scale

*Generated by `src/serving/q4_report.py` from `reports/q4_*.json`; full tables in `reports/q4_summary.md`.*

### 4.1 What was measured

We served the full two-stage pipeline for one request at a time: stage 1 retrieves up to 200 candidates (BM25 top-80 ∪ FAISS top-100 over A1 embeddings ∪ popularity top-20, from the circulating pool) and stage 2 re-ranks them with the Q3 popularity-aware NRMS. Everything a request reads is loaded once at start-up, including every article's NRMS vector, so a request never encodes text. Measurements ran on an Apple M4 CPU with PyTorch, FAISS and BLAS pinned to one thread. The served path reproduces the offline test scores (max difference 1e-06 on MIND, 4e-06 on EB-NeRD; identical top-1), so the numbers describe the evaluated model.

### 4.2 Memory

Serving needs **446 MB on MIND** and **169 MB on EB-NeRD**. The two largest items are per-article vectors: A1 embeddings for retrieval (100 MB) and NRMS article vectors for re-ranking (104 MB); NRMS weights are 68 MB. An exact FAISS index over MIND's whole catalogue is 100 MB; HNSW (M=32) adds 272 bytes per article (118 MB). The research process itself is far larger (1,485 MB MIND, 3,666 MB EB-NeRD) because the Q1/Q2 loaders parse raw files into Python objects and leave that memory reserved; isolated, EB-NeRD's word2vec loader keeps a 25 MB result but leaves 931 MB behind. A production server would load prebuilt serving artifacts instead.

### 4.3 Latency

Over 2,000 replayed test requests per dataset, one request takes **p50 1.14 ms / p99 2.24 ms on MIND** and **p50 1.74 ms / p99 3.81 ms on EB-NeRD**, far under a 100 ms p99 target; a second full run reproduced serving-mode p50–p99 within 5%. BM25 is the largest stage (35% of MIND's mean, 57% of EB-NeRD's) and sets the tail, because its query is built from the user's whole click history; NRMS re-ranking is a constant ~0.3 ms because it only scores 200 precomputed vectors. Calling the existing batch-evaluation functions per request instead (`as_is`) costs p99 29.6 ms on MIND (23.0× slower at p50): almost all of it is `build_queries` rebuilding a token dictionary over every article (p99 23.0 ms) and a Python scan of every article for popularity (2.1 ms), not the BM25 matrix itself (1.2 ms).

### 4.4 Cost

With one single-threaded worker per core at 60% utilisation and an assumed $0.04 per core-hour, 1,000 QPS needs **3 cores on MIND and 4 on EB-NeRD** (as_is MIND: 44), about **$0.00003 / $0.00004 per 1,000 queries**; 10,000 QPS needs 21 / 32 cores ($605 / $922 per month). A queueing simulation driven by the measured request times gives p99 2.5 ms (MIND) and 4.1 ms (EB-NeRD) at 1,000 QPS; MIND serving-mode p99 only reaches 10 ms at 95% utilisation, so the SLA is not the binding constraint — cost is. Even if a cloud vCPU were 3× slower than an M4 core, serving MIND at 10,000 QPS stays under 7 ms p99 with 61 cores. Worker RAM (0.81 GB MIND) fits within 4 GB per vCPU, so CPU sets the price today.

### 4.5 Where it breaks at 10×

We built a synthetic 10× catalogue (perturbed copies of every article; 65,238 → 652,380 on MIND) and replayed 1,000 real users. In order:

1. **Per-request code that touches every article.** `as_is` MIND p99 goes from 28 ms to **308 ms** and breaks the SLA on a single request (EB-NeRD: 91 ms, just under it with no headroom for queueing). Caching the request-independent parts removes this: serving p99 only grows 1.8 → 4.9 ms.
2. **RAM per worker.** Served structures grow 446 MB → 3,844 MB, so each MIND worker needs 4.2 GB — more than 4 GB per vCPU — and RAM rather than CPU sets the bill (60 vCPUs for 57 cores of work at 10× catalogue and 10× traffic). Fix: share read-only vectors across workers (memory-mapped files) or move them to a vector-search service.
3. **Approximate-search quality.** Exact search over the whole MIND catalogue grows to 18 ms p99 at 10×, pushing a larger site to HNSW — whose recall@100 falls from 0.81 to 0.46 at efSearch 64 (0.73 even at 256; EB-NeRD 0.97 → 0.89). Our design avoids this today by searching only the circulating pool (1.4 ms at 10×), but that pool grows with the site.
4. **Not the bottleneck:** stage-2 re-ranking (0.29 → 0.34 ms) and click-count lookups stay flat; 10× traffic alone is a linear cost (3 → 21 vCPUs) with lower p99 from larger pools. Not measured: ingesting 10× click events needs a streaming counter, and start-up (encoding every article, building indexes) grows linearly.

Caveats: laptop CPU (indicative per-core numbers), no network or remote stores in the timings, synthetic near-duplicate copies make 10× HNSW recall pessimistic and do not grow BM25's vocabulary, users ×10 is a linear memory extrapolation.
